then.text: The Famous Fake is in a glass case by the door, with a card that says exactly what it is. Visitors adore it. People always prefer an honest fake to a dishonest legend.
The sightings go back to the year 565, when St Columba is said to have seen off a beast in the River Ness. The loch keeps its secrets. We shall keep the receipts.
Shore, boatman, hunter, stall, ironmonger and the lady herself. Right. That's all my leads. Who made the photograph?

else.text: Still looking? Take your time. The 1934 photograph fooled people for sixty years, and it only took a toy submarine.

Ailsa Munro, archivist. I look after the Centre's photographs and my nerves.
A 'new' photograph of the monster has turned up, a long neck in black and white, very arty. We are about to put it on four thousand mugs.
You'll remember the famous one from 1934. It was exposed in the 1990s as a toy submarine with a head made of plastic wood. I'd like to be sure this one isn't the same joke told twice.
Three people had reason and chance. Have a look about. Your Fieldbook has a Casebook tab; press Run on the Fieldbook until it appears. A wrong accusation costs you standing.
Case opened: The Photograph.

then.text: A fake photograph? Oh, no. No no no. Who would do such a thing? I'm broken. Here, look at my notebook. I've drawn four hundred necks and not one of them was on purpose.
'Definitely a log, but what a log.' That's my professional opinion. I want the truth. The truth is out there. Somewhere. Probably in the loch.

monster_hunter.text: Nessie was first written about in the year 565, when St Columba ordered a water beast in the River Ness to leave a swimmer alone, and it did. That's the oldest sighting. The newest is probably this morning.
In 2018 scientists sampled the loch's water for DNA. They found a lot of eel. I'm choosing to believe it's one very large eel. Or a very friendly one.

castle_guide.text: Welcome to Urquhart. It's a ruin, but it's a well-organised ruin. That tower is the Grant Tower, and the view from the top is the best on the loch. There's a lift for the view. Lift: me. Shouting.
A Gaelic phrase, 'Fàilte gu Caisteal Urchadain'. Welcome to Urquhart Castle. Say it three times and the ghost of a medieval cook brings you a scone. Possibly.

coach_kid.text: I've been here forty minutes and I haven't seen the monster. I've seen a duck. The duck is quite large.
My gran says to watch the water for a V-shaped ripple, with nothing making it. I saw one. It was a swan. I felt a bit let down.

then.text: That the photograph? Aye. Look at the ripples, hen. Wee. Wee as a bath toy. A beast forty feet long makes a big fuss, and this made a polite one.
And that's my box camera in the cabin, if you're wondering. Wrong film, full of spiders. I took one picture with it in 1974 and it was of my thumb.

old_boatman.text: Fifty years on this loch, and I've never seen a monster. Mind you, I've never been looking. It's rude to stare.

The Caledonian Canal runs through the loch. It was built by Thomas Telford in the early 1800s, so ships could skip the long way round the north of Scotland. The loch's a motorway, to the right sort of boat.

then.text: I'm going. I'm already gone. This is an echo.

else.text: At the end of a wooden pier a survey boat bobs on the black water, loaded with sonar, a winch, a net the size of a tennis court and an urn of tea. Strachan stands at the rail.
Stand back from the gunwale. The Wardstone's in the water and the sonar says something very big is listening.
If you win, I lose my bonus. If I win, I lose my bonus anyway. Lord Vane's like that. Let's go.
A bubble breaks on the surface. Then another. The sonar on the boat gives a long, sad beep, like a microwave that has seen something.
The loch goes flat as a plate. A ring spreads out from the middle: one, two, three. Then something very long and very dark lifts through the water, shaped like a question mark with a sense of humour.
A head the size of a boat turns slowly towards the survey vessel. Two calm, ancient eyes. A long wet sigh. The net sinks without a ripple, and Nessie sneezes.
That. Is. Not. On. The. Sonar.
That is a long-necked aquatic mammal of unknown provenance, and I do not have a form for it. I have forms for everything. I have a form for forms.
Nessie looks at her, looks at you, and slides under the surface with hardly a bubble. The tea urn, for some reason, goes with her.
Right. That's it. That's the survey. I'm telling Head Office, and I'm telling them in writing. The Enclosure is pulling out of Scotland.
Tell Garside the Enclosure's pulling out of Scotland. We were never wanted here anyway. I'll take the boat back. Slowly. Something's following it.
The survey boat chugs away down the loch with a very wide wake and a very straight-backed Director on the foredeck. Far out, a long dark shape keeps pace, a hundred yards behind, rather politely.
Something deep in the loch has gone quiet, as if it were waiting for something cold. The Frost Stone, perhaps.

then.text: The island is quiet. Out on the loch, a ring of ripples spreads without a stone. Somewhere deep below it, someone is humming.

else.text: The island is dark with heather, and the loch is as still as a held breath. The Frost Stone grows cold in your pocket, and the water answers: a ring, then another.

A long neck rises out of the dark water, slow as a drawbridge. The head tilts. It has a sleepy, serious, enormous face, and the expression of a creature who has heard every joke about herself and loved most of them.

then.text: Nessie slides out of the loch and settles at your side, shedding peat-brown water like a silk coat. Down on the shore, a day-tripper drops her ice cream. She'll be telling people about this for forty years.

else.text: Nessie sinks without a sound, and the loch smooths itself over like a duvet. She will be back on a quiet day, if you want to try again.
The island is dark with heather, and the water around it is black and very cold. A long shadow turns over, deep down, and then thinks better of it.
Whatever lives here only answers something as cold and as patient as it is. Perhaps the Keeper in Inverness has the kind of Stone it is waiting for.
The island is quiet. Out on the loch, the Enclosure survey boat is still circling. Whatever lives down there isn't coming up while that thing's out.
